title: Here am I (Isaiah 6:1–8)
hookLine: Isaiah sees the Lord high and lifted up, and says here am I, send me

lines: A THRONE, HIGH AND LIFTED UP.
cards: It begins with a date: "In the year that king Uzziah died." A king is dead, and a whole kingdom is waiting to see what comes next. In that year, a man named Isaiah is in the Temple in Jerusalem, and he sees something.
The Lord, sitting on a throne, high and lifted up, the hem of his robe filling the whole Temple. Above him, beings with six wings each, calling to one another. The doorposts shake.

teach.b: The text calls these beings seraphim, a name some readers link to a Hebrew word for burning.
With two wings they cover their faces, with two their feet, and with two they fly, and they call: "Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory."
Churches still sing that line in the Sanctus at communion, and in hymns. Isaiah's first reaction isn't wonder.
It's terror: "Woe is me! for I am undone; because I am a man of unclean lips." Not terrible deeds: an unclean mouth, the very thing a prophet needs.

teach.h: A LIVE COAL ON THE MOUTH.
teach.b: Then one of the seraphim flies to the altar, takes a live coal with tongs, and touches it to his lips. Your guilt is taken away, it says.
Now, at last, a question from the throne, and it isn't a command: "Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?" And Isaiah: "Here am I; send me."

In Hebrew that's hineni, one short word: here I am. Abraham says it when God calls him, Moses at the burning bush, the boy Samuel in the night. It doesn't mean I'm qualified; Isaiah has just said he isn't.
And it comes before he knows the job. The next verses give him a hard message for a people who won't listen. He says yes first.
Christians hear their own calls in this scene at ordinations and sendings for mission, and in ordinary moments too: someone asks who will go, and a hand goes up.

how: Christians sing the seraphim's 'Holy, holy, holy' in the Sanctus of the communion service, and Isaiah 6 is often read at ordinations and when people are commissioned for mission or service.

o: I'm ready because I'm fully qualified
here I am: present, listening, available
a cry of fear before something holy

games.q: what's inside the call — tap the pairs.

s: God asks a question: whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Isaiah volunteers.
Isaiah says yes before he hears the message
"here am I; send me" comes first. the hard job is described afterward.
hineni is said only by Isaiah
Abraham, Moses and the boy Samuel say it too when God calls.

games.q: you've just seen the Lord on a throne and felt your own unworthiness. a voice asks: whom shall I send? what do you say?
o: I'm not good enough: send someone else.
first tell me what the job is.
games.why: Isaiah says "here am I; send me," right after saying he's a man of unclean lips. he answers before he knows the job.

practice: Notice where you are right now, the chair, the room, the sounds, the light, and let yourself be fully here, the way hineni means.
Then think of one place this week where someone is asking, in their own way, who will go, a neighbor, a coworker, a family member, a cause, and simply turn toward it; you don't have to fix it.
If you pray, you can say Isaiah's words, here am I, send me; if you don't, simply say here I am, and mean it.

wordCard.voice: Hineni. Hebrew for here I am, the answer of Abraham, Moses, Samuel and Isaiah, said present and available, before any of them knew the job.

orig.note: Hebrew: here I am. one word, said by Abraham, Moses, Samuel and Isaiah when called.

carryVoice: Your line: send me. Present first, and the job comes after that. See you tomorrow.
